*An update to "The Architecture of Profit". This one is about Progress Ireland: where I agree with them, where I don't, and something about how they operate that bothers me. It's a separate post because it responds to work and reporting that came out after the series went up.*

---

## Where we agree

Progress Ireland and I are looking at the same thing, and I want to say so up front because the disagreements below land harder for it.

Their October 2026 piece on housing-infrastructure funding gets to the same place as my series. Rezoned land in Dublin went from roughly €60,000 to €1.6 million per hectare in 2024, a 27-fold jump that their author puts down mostly to a public decision and public investment. That is my land-value-capture argument in different words, from the same CSO sources. Their fix is land readjustment: pool the land in a development area, replot it, and use reserve land to pay for the infrastructure. It's one of the more concrete versions of the Kenny-report principle I've seen in recent Irish policy writing. I documented what gets captured and showed that no official body has measured it. They've supplied part of how you'd give it back. On this, they're allies.

## Where we don't, part one: the policy

Progress Ireland was the loudest advocate for exempting back-garden modular homes from planning. The "shedsits". As of April 2026 they're exempt not only from planning permission but, through an extension of the rent-a-room scheme, from the Residential Tenancies Board too. The think tank said the measure could deliver up to 350,000 homes.

I think it's a bad policy, and the cost falls almost entirely on the people it's meant to help. The Irish Planning Institute raised eight objections, including that the units would drift into short-term letting and that garden potential would push house prices up for first-time buyers. Threshold and housing academics warned that rented units like these would be nearly impossible to police for standards. Opposition leaders from three parties compared it to a return of tenements and bedsits.

Take away the planning check and the tenancy-standards check and the gain goes to whoever owns the garden, while the tenant carries the risk. An advocate can still point to it as a win because the costs are spread out, show up later, and land on tenants with the least power to say no. It adds a line to a delivery chart. It doesn't add a home anyone should have to live in. It's the build-anything-at-any-quality instinct, with nobody asking who pays, which is exactly the instinct this whole series is about.

## Where we don't, part two: the transparency problem

This one is more serious.

Progress Ireland is funded by two billionaires. When an Oireachtas committee asked how much, they declined to say. A lot of their influence also runs through private channels to senior officials. Given what my series is about, I'm wary of that.

The record is specific. In December 2025 an assistant secretary general at the Department of Further and Higher Education sent a Progress Ireland staff member a confidential draft funding framework: the assessment criteria for university bids under a €750 million programme. The official marked it for review "on a strictly confidential basis", after a sister department had asked that it not be published. Progress Ireland's board includes that official's former secretary general. Then in October 2026 it emerged that the Department of Housing's new housing tsar had met a Progress Ireland lobbyist and nobody kept a record.

None of that is allegation. It comes from freedom-of-information requests. To be fair, minuting that meeting was the official's and the department's job, not the think tank's, and Progress Ireland's lobbying returns are on the public register, so they aren't wholly opaque. Part of what the record shows is poor record-keeping by officials, not by the lobbyist. But put it together: funding they won't put a number on, a confidential draft that travelled through a board connection, an unminuted meeting with a newly appointed official. That's a well-funded interest getting quiet, privileged access to the people who write the rules. It's the same imbalance I describe elsewhere in the series, just with a different cast.

It doesn't matter that they're lobbying for some things I agree with. You find out whether you believe in transparent policy-making when it's an ally doing it. Billionaire-funded access to officials that nobody can see is undemocratic when the Construction Industry Federation does it, and it's undemocratic when a think tank I often agree with does it.

## Where that leaves me

I'm not dismissing them. Their research is often rigorous, they compare across countries usefully, and on land value capture they're pushing in the direction the evidence points. They could do a lot of good in Irish housing policy.

They'd do it better, and their arguments would carry more weight, if they put their funding and their meetings with officials under the same daylight they ask of the planning system. If you want the state to capture privately held value for the public, letting the public see who funds you and who you meet shouldn't be hard.
